definition: The company invests minority equity stakes in external companies, startups, or early-stage ventures — whether through a named CVC fund, direct balance-sheet investments, or non-marketable equity securities. The investment may be strategic (aligned with business goals) or financial. Evidence includes: equity investments in private companies, venture fund operations, non-marketable securities on the balance sheet, investment income from equity stakes, or references to strategic minority investments.

The company runs or participates in structured programmes that support early-stage companies or internal ventures through resources, guidance, and infrastructure. Evidence includes: named accelerator or incubator programmes, startup cohort support, innovation labs or sandboxes, moonshot or internal incubation structures (e.g. X, Other Bets), seed-stage investment with active support, or structured startup competitions and challenge programmes.

The company creates and scales new businesses from within, operating them as independent or semi-independent entities. Evidence includes: internal new business creation, subsidiary ventures with their own boards/investors, moonshot projects developing into standalone companies, spin-outs, new product lines operating as separate business units, or named internal ventures (e.g. Waymo, Isomorphic Labs, Kuiper).

The company acts as a customer, partner, or commercial counterparty for startups or emerging technology companies, validating and scaling their solutions. Evidence includes: strategic partnerships with startups, commercial agreements alongside equity investment, procurement from early-stage companies, joint development agreements, references to using startup technology in operations, or statements that acquisitions and strategic investments are important to the business.

The company provides guidance, expertise, or advisory support to ventures, startups, or internal innovators. Evidence includes: executive involvement with portfolio companies, advisory board participation, training and capability-building programmes for entrepreneurs, expert access programmes, coaching or support for founders, or internal programmes developing entrepreneurial talent.

The company provides operational resources, technology, infrastructure, or capabilities that help ventures and businesses grow. Evidence includes: cloud computing platforms, developer tools, AI/ML infrastructure, distribution or marketplace access, supply chain or logistics services, data or analytics tools, or any platform described as helping customers build, scale, or run their businesses — including enterprise customers who may be startups.

The company provides physical or digital environments that enable ventures or teams to work and innovate. Evidence includes: innovation labs, R&D campuses, co-working or incubator facilities, digital collaboration platforms (e.g. productivity suites, developer environments), data centers or computing infrastructure used by businesses, or any dedicated space or digital environment provided for innovation or business operations.

The company hosts, sponsors, or participates in gatherings that connect innovators, developers, or the startup ecosystem. Evidence includes: developer conferences, innovation summits, hackathons, demo days, startup competitions, community events, partner or ecosystem gatherings, or any structured event designed to build relationships with external innovators or showcase new technology.

Risk Management as a corporate venturing objective refers to using venturing activities to reduce, hedge, or distribute risk across the innovation portfolio. By investing in multiple early-stage companies across different technology trajectories, corporations create a hedge against disruptive technology risk — if any single approach wins, the corporate has exposure to it. Venturing activities can also reduce market concentration risk, supplier dependency risk, and technology obsolescence risk.

Market Expansion as a corporate venturing objective refers to using venturing activities — investments, partnerships, venture building — to enter new geographic markets, customer segments, or product categories faster or at lower risk than organic growth alone would allow.

Access to New Technology, as a corporate venturing objective, refers to the use of CV practices and activities to identify, acquire, develop, and deploy technologies that are beyond the current capabilities of the corporation's internal R&D function — particularly emerging, disruptive, or frontier technologies whose development trajectories are difficult to predict and whose internal development would be too slow, too costly, or too culturally difficult to sustain.

Develop Business Ecosystems, as a corporate venturing objective, refers to the deliberate use of CV practices and activities to build, expand, and orchestrate a network of interdependent companies, developers, partners, suppliers, and customers whose collective activities create value that no single participant could generate alone — and from which the corporation derives disproportionate strategic and economic benefit as the ecosystem orchestrator or keystone player.

Social and Environmental Impact, as a corporate venturing objective, refers to the deliberate orientation of CV practices and activities toward generating measurable positive outcomes for society and the natural environment — alongside or in place of purely financial or competitive objectives. This encompasses climate technology investment, social equity initiatives, community development, and the application of venturing capital and expertise to problems that market forces alone have historically under-addressed.

Developing Entrepreneurial Culture and Capabilities, as a corporate venturing objective, refers to the use of CV practices and activities to transform the internal culture, mindset, skills, and organisational processes of the corporation toward greater speed, experimentation, risk tolerance, founder- orientation, and innovation agility — qualities that characterise successful startups and that large organisations systematically lose as they scale.

Financial Return, as a corporate venturing objective, refers to the explicit pursuit of direct monetary gains from corporate venturing activities — including capital appreciation on equity investments, realized gains on exits (IPOs, acquisitions, secondary sales), dividend income from portfolio companies, licensing royalties, carried interest, and the measurable revenue and margin uplift attributable to venturing activities.
